Drag the timeline to explore dates without changing that duration. The arrows shift by one window width, or 100 years at this scale.\n\nThe slider jumps quickly to another date between 4000 BCE and the present. “4000 BCE → now” restores the overview. Dragging and pinching within this range stay within its bounds; use −, the scale menu or search to reach prehistoric landmarks. Nearby records are grouped when their labels would overlap; open a group to read its records or zoom closer.
Smithsonian · Homo sapiens
Homo sapiens in Africa

Fossils place the emergence of our species in Africa around 300,000 years ago. This begins the human-history overview here. Human evolution is much older, and other human species also lived during part of this long period.
An approximate fossil-based landmark, not the date of a single first human or a sudden birth of culture.
National Museum of Australia · Sahul
Peopling Sahul

People reached the landmass that then joined Australia and New Guinea after crossing sea passages from Southeast Asia. These migrations began a very long history of Aboriginal societies adapting to diverse environments.
The museum gives an arrival estimate between 65,000 and 50,000 years ago. This is dating uncertainty, not the duration of Aboriginal cultures.
UNESCO · Çatalhöyük
Çatalhöyük: settled life

In Anatolia, tightly packed houses, wall paintings and successive occupation layers reveal a large settled community. Access through roofs and rebuilt homes show a form of collective life different from a modern street-based town.
The range concerns the eastern Neolithic mound. The western mound continues later; it does not date the invention of agriculture.
Getty · Mesopotamia
Mesopotamia: cities and writing

Urban institutions grew in southern Mesopotamia. Administrative records helped manage goods and labour, while writing developed from early signs into more elaborate systems. Cities, specialised work and monumental buildings transformed collective organisation.
This range describes an early urban and written-record phase in Mesopotamia, not a simultaneous worldwide beginning of history.
UNESCO · Dholavira
Dholavira and the Indus world

Dholavira, in present-day Gujarat, combined fortified spaces, workshops and carefully organised water storage. Its long occupation illustrates the changing urban societies of the Indus region and their ability to manage scarce water.
Approximate occupation range for this particular site, covering several Harappan phases rather than one unchanging civilisation.
UNESCO · Caral-Supe
Caral-Supe in the Andes

On the Peruvian coast, Caral-Supe developed monumental platforms, plazas and organised ceremonial spaces. It provides an early American example of large collective construction and complex settlement, alongside other independent urban histories.
The range follows the archaeological development described for the site; it is not the age of the first settlement of the Americas.
The Met · Egypt, Old Kingdom
Egypt’s Old Kingdom

Royal administration and funerary complexes expanded along the Nile. The pyramids belong to a society of specialised labour, religious institutions and powerful royal households. Much surviving evidence comes from tombs, which gives an uneven view of everyday life.
Approximate chronology used by this museum synthesis. These boundaries delimit the Old Kingdom, not all of ancient Egypt, whose history continues for over two millennia.
The Met · Shang and Zhou
Shang China

In the Yellow River region, Shang rulers relied on centres of political and ritual power. Bronze vessels reveal highly specialised casting and the importance of offerings to ancestors. Other contemporary cultures also developed elsewhere in what is now China.
A dynastic range, not the beginning or the whole history of Chinese societies.
The Met · Han dynasty
Han China

Han governments consolidated imperial administration while cities, scholarship and diplomacy developed. Exchange across Central Asia connected the empire with distant societies. Its history includes major political breaks and the move from a western to an eastern capital.
The overall range includes the interruption between the Western Han, ending in 9 CE, and Eastern Han, beginning in 25 CE.
The Met · Roman Empire
Rome and the Mediterranean

Imperial Rome linked territories around the Mediterranean through administration, cities and trade, backed by conquest and military power. Over time its political centres and institutions changed. The end of imperial rule in the West did not end Roman history in the East.
27 BCE marks Augustus; 476 marks a conventional western endpoint. The Eastern Roman Empire continued until 1453.
The Met · Classic Maya
Classic Maya cities

Maya city-states formed shifting alliances and rivalries across Mesoamerica. Royal courts supported monumental art and writing that recorded historical and sacred narratives. These societies shared cultural traditions without forming one permanently unified empire.
Approximate limits of the Classic period. They do not delimit the existence of Maya peoples, who continue today.
The Met · Tang dynasty
Tang cities and exchanges

The Tang capital brought together merchants, religious communities and envoys from many regions. Poetry, painting and administration flourished within an empire also shaped by wars and rebellions. Its routes supported exchanges of objects, practices and ideas.
A dynastic range; cultural exchanges and traditions extend beyond these political boundaries.
The Met · Umayyad period
The Umayyad caliphate

The Umayyad caliphate governed a large and diverse territory from Damascus. Arabic administration and new religious monuments developed alongside artistic traditions inherited from earlier societies. Political expansion did not instantly erase local cultures.
These dates concern the Damascus-based caliphate, not the beginning or the full history of Islam.
UNESCO · Angkor
Angkor and the Khmer world

Successive Khmer capitals formed a vast landscape of temples, settlements and water infrastructure. Angkor’s monuments show religious and artistic transformations over centuries. The archaeological landscape also remains inhabited.
A rounded window for the ninth to fifteenth centuries, not exact foundation and abandonment dates.
UNESCO · Great Zimbabwe
Great Zimbabwe

Large dry-stone enclosures and hill settlements testify to a major centre of southern African society. Their construction required considerable organisation and skill. The monument belongs to the history of local African populations.
Approximate construction range for the monumental site, not the duration of all settlement in the region.
Te Ara · Māori settlement
Settlement of Aotearoa

Voyagers from East Polynesia reached Aotearoa New Zealand through purposeful ocean navigation. Their descendants developed Māori societies. Winds, currents and celestial observations supported journeys over enormous sea distances.
Estimated interval for initial settlement, not the lifespan of Māori societies.
The Met · Sahel and trans-Saharan exchange
Mansa Musa and Saharan routes

The ruler of Mali travelled to Mecca through Cairo. His pilgrimage highlights the place of West African states within long-distance commercial, religious and diplomatic networks. Gold and salt were among the goods moving across the Sahara.
1324 is the pilgrimage landmark, not the foundation of Mali or of trans-Saharan trade.
SlaveVoyages · Transatlantic estimates
The transatlantic slave trade

The forced transport of enslaved Africans linked African coasts, European commercial powers and American colonies. Violence, family separation and coerced labour shaped this system; enslaved people resisted it in many ways.
1501–1866 is the coverage of the database’s estimates. These are not universal beginning and ending dates for slavery.
Science Museum · Steam and industry
Britain’s industrial transformation

Stationary steam engines supplied mechanical power before railways became widespread. Factory production and the use of coal transformed work and manufacturing in Britain. Other regions industrialised at different times and through different paths.
The museum uses 1760–1830 for this British phase. It is not a worldwide industrial timetable.
US National Archives · Declaration of Independence
Declaration of American independence

Thirteen British colonies declared themselves independent states. The declaration stated political principles and grievances against the Crown. Its adoption was one stage in a longer war and did not mean that equal rights were already enjoyed by everyone.
The declaration was adopted on 4 July 1776; the principal signing took place on 2 August.
Assemblée nationale · Declaration of 1789
France: rights and revolution

The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen asserted liberty, legal equality and national sovereignty during the French Revolution. Its principles opened lasting political struggles over who could actually exercise these rights.
The articles were voted from 20 to 26 August 1789. A declaration of principle is distinct from its application.
UNESCO · Haitian independence
Haitian independence

Following a struggle rooted in revolt against slavery and colonial rule, Haiti proclaimed independence. The new state challenged the Atlantic colonial order. The Citadel and other monuments testify to efforts to defend this hard-won independence.
The proclamation dates to 1 January 1804; the revolution and the struggles over abolition began earlier.
Princeton University Art Museum · Meiji Japan
Meiji Japan

Japan underwent major political and social transformations during the Meiji era. New technologies and international contacts reshaped cities and visual culture. Contemporary prints also document the growth of Japanese military power and imperial ambitions.
The dates delimit an imperial era, not a single industrial event or a universal model of modernisation.
Imperial War Museums · First World War
The First World War

A conflict originating in Europe mobilised people and resources across empires and continents. Its scale involved industrial armies and civilian societies alike. The fighting and its consequences transformed political orders far beyond the European fronts.
1914–1918 are the usual war bounds. Peace settlements and regional violence continued after the armistices.
USHMM · World War II
The Second World War

Nazi Germany’s expansion opened a war in Europe that became part of a global conflict. Occupation, mass violence and destruction devastated civilian societies. The Holocaust unfolded within this wartime setting while pursuing the Nazi regime’s antisemitic project.
1939 marks the war’s conventional European opening. Conflicts in Asia had already begun; 1945 does not end every local conflict.
USHMM · Holocaust overview
The Holocaust

The Nazi regime, its allies and collaborators persecuted and murdered Europe’s Jews. Six million Jews were killed. Discrimination and exclusion escalated into mass murder. Other populations were also targeted by Nazi persecution and killing policies.
This range includes persecution from 1933; it does not mean the same policies or level of killing operated throughout.
United Nations · Founding history
Founding of the United Nations

The United Nations was created after the Second World War to provide a framework for international cooperation and collective security. Its institutions gave states a shared forum, without removing conflicts of interest or unequal power.
The Charter was signed on 26 June 1945 and entered into force on 24 October.
UK National Archives · Partition of British India
Independence and Partition

British rule ended as India and Pakistan became independent. Partition divided territories and communities and was accompanied by immense population movements and violence. Independence and displacement are inseparable parts of this history.
The landmark concerns British India in 1947, not a single worldwide end to colonial rule.
United Nations · Universal Declaration
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights

Representatives with different legal and cultural backgrounds drafted a common statement of human rights. Adopted by the UN General Assembly, it became a central reference for later agreements and campaigns for equality and dignity.
Adopted on 10 December 1948. Adoption of a declaration does not mean its principles are universally enforced.
United Nations · Decolonization
Decolonisation: a UN declaration

The UN General Assembly called for independence for colonial countries and peoples. This landmark belonged to broader struggles already pursued by colonised populations. Decolonisation transformed the international system through varied, often conflictual paths.
1960 dates the declaration, not the beginning or completion of every decolonisation process.
NASA · Apollo 11
Apollo 11: humans on the Moon

Apollo 11 brought the first people to the lunar surface. The mission combined scientific work, engineering and a vast industrial effort. It also belonged to the political competition of the space age.
The lunar landing occurred on 20 July 1969. The first steps were on 21 July in UTC.
CERN · The birth of the Web
The birth of the Web

Tim Berners-Lee proposed a system for linking information at CERN. Browsers, servers and hypertext made documents accessible across computers. Releasing the software helped the Web spread beyond its original research setting.
1989 marks the proposal; CERN released the software into the public domain on 30 April 1993. The Web is not the same as the older Internet.
South African Government · Democratic elections
South Africa’s democratic elections

The first democratic national elections open to all racial groups marked the transition away from apartheid rule. They followed long struggles and negotiations. Political change did not instantly remove the social and economic consequences of segregation.
27 April is the commemorative landmark for the 1994 elections, not the start or end of every struggle against apartheid.
UNFCCC · Paris Agreement
The Paris Agreement

Countries adopted a common framework for responding to climate change through national commitments and international cooperation. The agreement became a major landmark in climate diplomacy. An agreement’s adoption is distinct from achieving its goals.
Adopted on 12 December 2015; entry into force followed in 2016.

History and sciences · references and dating

These reading windows are editorial guides, not universal historical periods. Their boundaries do not imply that societies changed together. Dates use BCE/CE without a civil year zero; the oldest landmarks use rounded ages. The displayed horizon is fixed at 2026. The overview starts with Homo sapiens; earlier human evolution remains outside this selection.

Each landmark identifies a place, an event or a documented interval. Dating uncertainty, a dynasty, a site’s occupation and the coverage of an archive are different things; the notes distinguish them. A line clipped by the visible window continues beyond it. The region filter selects only the regions explicitly attached to each record; “Worldwide” is a separate category.

This is an expandable selection, not an exhaustive world history. Missing records do not mean a region had no history. The texts are original summaries; source texts and photographs are not imported. Drawings are generic symbols, not archaeological reconstructions.
Human history

Follow our species from its emergence in Africa to a world of connected societies. Most of this immense span precedes cities and writing. People developed diverse ways of living, travelling and passing on knowledge.\n\nThe first zoom separates long histories of foraging, the growth of settled communities, and roughly the last 5,000 years. These are reading windows, not steps that every society followed. This first selection brings together dated examples from several continents and will be expanded.
Foragers and migrations

For most of our species’ history, people obtained food from wild resources and moved in many different ways. Migrations carried communities into new environments, including lands reached across water. Archaeology preserves fragments of these histories rather than a continuous record.\n\nThe window ends at a convenient chronological boundary. Hunting, gathering and mobile societies did not disappear with the emergence of farming.
Villages and farming

During the millennia following the last glacial period, settled communities and food production expanded through different regional histories. Changes in housing, work and social organisation accumulated over generations. Sedentary life and farming did not always begin together.\n\nThe selected examples move from a large Anatolian settlement to Mesopotamian cities and early writing. They illustrate particular trajectories, not a single worldwide invention.
About 5,000 years

This zoom brings recent millennia into view without losing their place in the longer timeline. Urban societies, states and exchange networks have very different histories in different regions. Written records enrich our knowledge but remain partial, alongside archaeology and oral traditions.\n\nThree broad windows lead to early urban worlds, regional networks and empires, then increasingly interconnected modern histories. Their titles describe themes, not a ranking of societies.
Early urban worlds

Large settlements and centres of power developed in several regions. Managing water, organising labour, making specialised objects and building monuments took different forms along the Nile, in the Indus region, in China and on the Andean coast.\n\nCompare the dated examples below: overlapping timelines do not mean identical institutions, direct contact or a common origin. Many people continued to live outside cities.
Empires and exchanges

Over these centuries, large political formations and regional networks connected many societies while remaining uneven and changeable. Routes carried goods and knowledge, and could also carry armies, coerced labour and epidemics.\n\nThe next two windows place Mediterranean, Asian, African, American and Oceanian examples on the same time axis. The familiar European divide between Antiquity and the Middle Ages is not treated as a global boundary.
Cities and imperial powers

The Mediterranean under Rome and China under the Han offer two examples of extensive imperial systems. Elsewhere, societies organised power differently, including the Maya city-states of Mesoamerica. Their histories overlap but do not share one timetable.\n\nPolitical dates are useful anchors. They rarely mark the abrupt beginning or disappearance of a population, language or cultural tradition.
Connected regional worlds

Caravan routes, sea voyages and diplomatic or religious journeys connected distant communities. Tang China, the Umayyad caliphate, Angkor, Great Zimbabwe and Mali illustrate different centres of power and exchange. Polynesian navigation extended settlement across the Pacific.\n\nThis panorama avoids reducing a millennium to one European story. Each selected site or journey is a point of entry into a much larger regional history.
An interconnected world

Oceanic connections, colonial expansion, industrialisation and political struggles increasingly reshaped relations between continents. These connections included both voluntary exchanges and extreme coercion, especially slavery and conquest.\n\nFiner windows make recent centuries readable. They separate broad contexts without claiming that industrialisation, independence or access to rights happened everywhere at the same time.
Oceans and revolutions

Atlantic economies tied distant regions together through trade, colonisation and the forced transport of enslaved people. Political declarations at the end of the eighteenth century challenged forms of authority while leaving major exclusions in place.\n\nBritain’s industrial transformation also began within this window. Processes that cross its boundaries keep their full dates in their individual records.
Industries and empires

Industrial production, transport and military power changed relations between states and societies. These transformations followed unequal regional paths. Meiji Japan illustrates one such reorganisation; Haitian independence illustrates a different struggle over freedom and sovereignty.\n\nIndustrial development did not end coercion. The transatlantic slave trade continued into the nineteenth century, alongside abolitionist struggles.
World wars and mass violence

Two world wars mobilised societies on an immense scale. Military fronts, occupation, displacement and mass violence deeply affected civilian life. Nazi persecution developed into the Holocaust, in which six million Jews were murdered.\n\nThe records distinguish the chronology of wars from that of persecution. A war’s conventional start or end does not capture all the violence experienced in every region.
Rights and independences

After 1945, international institutions and declarations set new frameworks for cooperation and rights. Decolonisation reshaped the political map through struggles and negotiations, sometimes accompanied by severe violence and displacement.\n\nScientific achievements such as the first lunar landing developed amid international competition. Shared institutions and technical progress did not eliminate inequality or conflict.
Networks and shared challenges

The spread of the Web transformed access to information and communication. Political transitions, including South Africa’s democratic elections, changed institutions without immediately resolving inherited inequalities. International climate diplomacy addressed problems crossing national borders.\n\nThis window ends at the fixed 2026 horizon. Its selected records provide historical anchors; they are not a live news feed or an exhaustive account of recent decades.

NMEC · Egyptian chronology
Egypt: from the first dynasties to Rome

This broad band follows Egyptian kingdoms from early unification to Roman annexation. The Old Kingdom is only one phase: reunifications, divided rule and foreign dynasties follow. Egyptian society and traditions continue under Rome.
An approximate starting landmark and a political endpoint, not the beginning and disappearance of a people. Intermediate periods are included in this overview.
The Met · Middle Kingdom
Egypt’s Middle Kingdom

After political fragmentation, royal reunification opens a new phase of Egyptian history. Kingship, religious practice, literature and sculpture change. Royal temple building expands, while many surviving objects reveal more intimate aspects of belief and elite life.
Approximate chronology from the museum’s revised essay. These boundaries differ between scholarly chronologies.
The Met · New Kingdom
Egypt’s New Kingdom

Reunification under Ahmose begins a period of territorial expansion and major royal building projects. Temples, royal tombs and diplomatic contacts reflect Egypt’s reach into Nubia and the Near East. Religious and political changes make this a varied era rather than a single unchanging system.
Approximate boundaries for Dynasties 18–20. The end of the New Kingdom is not the end of ancient Egypt.
The Met · Late Period
Egypt’s Late Period

Egyptian dynasties and periods of Persian rule alternate. Temples, sculpture and religious practices develop through renewed engagement with older traditions. Alexander’s conquest marks the political transition to Macedonian rule.
The date range follows the museum’s revised chronology. This period includes Persian domination, not only Egyptian dynasties.
The Met · Hellenistic Egypt
From Alexander to Cleopatra VII

Alexander’s conquest is followed by Macedonian rulers and the Ptolemaic dynasty. Alexandria becomes a major royal and cultural centre. Greek and Egyptian traditions interact, while Egyptian temples remain important. Cleopatra VII belongs to the end of this long history.
The window starts with Alexander in 332 BCE; the Ptolemaic dynasty itself starts in 305 BCE. Roman annexation follows in 30 BCE.
The Met · Roman Egypt
Egypt comes under Roman rule

After the defeat of Antony and Cleopatra VII, Octavian takes control of Egypt. The former kingdom becomes a Roman province. Egyptian religious and artistic traditions continue alongside changes in administration and connections with the wider empire.
A change of political authority, not an abrupt end to Egyptian civilization.
Egyptian Ministry of Antiquities · Great Pyramid
Khufu and the Great Pyramid

The Great Pyramid at Giza was built as Khufu’s tomb. Limestone masonry, internal passages and burial chambers required a major building effort. The ministry estimates a construction period of ten to twenty years, while the exact building techniques remain debated.
The band gives Khufu’s approximate reign according to this source. These are not known opening and completion dates for the building site.
English Heritage · Stonehenge
Stonehenge: raising the stone circle

The large stone circle belongs to a major phase in a much longer building history. Its builders worked within a landscape already used for monuments and burial. The origins and transport of the stones are central archaeological questions.
An approximate landmark for the stone circle, not the first work on the site, which began around 3000 BCE.
Acropolis Museum · Parthenon
Building the Parthenon

On the Athenian Acropolis, a temple dedicated to Athena combines architecture with a large sculptural programme. Its reliefs and pediments express religious traditions and the city’s public identity. Later uses and damage transform the building over the centuries.
The range covers construction and the sculptural programme. It does not describe the building’s entire period of use.
Roma Capitale · Colosseum
The Colosseum opens in Rome

The Flavian amphitheatre opens under Titus after work begun under Vespasian. Public spectacles bring large crowds into a building organized around entrances, seating and an arena. Its construction also reshapes an area previously occupied by Nero’s imperial estate.
80 CE is the opening date. Construction began in the preceding decade, and later alterations continued after inauguration.
The Met · Hagia Sophia
Building Hagia Sophia

Justinian’s cathedral in Constantinople brings together a vast interior, an ambitious dome and rich decoration. The structure becomes a major reference in architectural history. Earthquakes, repairs and changes of use subsequently alter parts of the monument.
Dates for the sixth-century building campaign, not for all structures on the site or every element visible today.
UNESCO · Borobudur
Borobudur: a Buddhist monument

In central Java, terraces, reliefs and stupas organize a monumental Buddhist complex. Architecture and sculpted narratives work together along a route through the building. Borobudur illustrates the importance of religious patronage and skilled workshops in the region.
Rounded window for the eighth and ninth centuries cited by UNESCO, not two exact dates or a continuous two-century building site.
French Ministry of Culture · Notre-Dame
Notre-Dame: the medieval building campaigns

Successive generations of builders raise the Paris cathedral and transform its design. The long programme includes the choir, nave, façades and later medieval alterations. Notre-Dame’s subsequent history brings further modifications and restorations.
Conventional range for most medieval construction. It does not mean uninterrupted work or a monument unchanged after 1345.
UNESCO · Machu Picchu
Machu Picchu in the Inca world

In the Andes, stone buildings and agricultural terraces form a complex adapted to a steep mountain site. Paths and water management connect its spaces. Its construction belongs to the history of the Inca Empire, well before the site’s modern international fame.
A rounded fifteenth-century construction window, following UNESCO. It is not an exact foundation date or a century of continuous building.
UNESCO · Imperial palaces of China
Building Beijing’s Forbidden City

Under the Ming emperor Yongle, a vast palace complex is built in Beijing. Gates, courtyards and ceremonial halls organize imperial authority in space. The palace later serves the Qing court and undergoes numerous repairs and reconstructions.
The first major construction campaign in Beijing, not the dates of every surviving building or of the Shenyang palace.
UNESCO · Taj Mahal
Taj Mahal: building the funerary complex

Shah Jahan commissions a mausoleum at Agra in memory of Mumtaz Mahal. The marble tomb, gardens and surrounding buildings combine architecture, stone inlay and calligraphy. The mausoleum is completed before the wider ensemble.
The detailed UNESCO chronology gives 1632–1648 for the mausoleum and 1653 for later buildings. Its introductory summary places the start in 1631.
Eiffel Tower · Construction history
Building the Eiffel Tower

Built for the 1889 Paris world’s fair, the tower assembles iron components prepared in workshops. Its construction combines careful design, prefabrication and work high above the city. The summit is completed on 31 March 1889.
Construction dates, not the date of the design competition or the later opening to visitors.
Sydney Opera House · Building history
Building the Sydney Opera House

The Bennelong Point project turns an ambitious architectural design into a performing-arts complex. Its long construction requires major engineering work and successive changes. The building opens in 1973 and becomes a landmark of the harbour.
The range runs from the start of construction to opening, excluding earlier design work and later renovation campaigns.
British Museum · Muwatalli II and Kadesh
The Battle of Kadesh

Ramesses II’s Egyptian army confronts the Hittite forces of Muwatalli II at Kadesh. The battle places Egypt within the rivalries of the eastern Mediterranean and the Near East. It is a military episode within the New Kingdom, not the end of that period.
Conventional year in the chronology used here. Its conversion from ancient regnal dates remains approximate.
English Heritage · Battle of Hastings
The Battle of Hastings

William of Normandy defeats King Harold’s army in southern England. Harold’s death and the Norman victory open a new phase of the struggle for control of the kingdom. Conquest and the consolidation of royal power continue after the battle.
A battle on 14 October 1066, not a one-day completion of the Norman conquest.
BnF · Hundred Years’ War
The Hundred Years’ War

A succession of conflicts pits the kingdoms of France and England against each other, alongside changing alliances and internal struggles. Campaigns, sieges and raids affect towns and countryside. Long truces interrupt the fighting.
A conventional 116-year framework, not one hundred years or a continuous battle.
National Army Museum · Waterloo
The Battle of Waterloo

Napoleon’s army faces the coalition forces led by Wellington and Blücher in present-day Belgium. The French defeat ends the military campaign of the Hundred Days and leads to Napoleon’s second abdication.
The battle took place on 18 June 1815. It is one event within the much longer Revolutionary and Napoleonic wars.
US National Park Service · Civil War
The American Civil War

Secession leads to war between the Union and the Confederacy. Slavery is central to the crisis. Union victory preserves the United States, while abolition becomes enshrined in the Thirteenth Amendment. Reconstruction brings further struggles over citizenship and rights.
The military conflict’s conventional years. Surrenders were staggered in 1865; its social and political consequences extend far beyond.
Verdun Memorial · The battle
The Battle of Verdun

German and French armies fight around Verdun in a prolonged battle dominated by artillery, forts and repeated attacks. The losses and destruction make Verdun a major place of remembrance. Later commemorations also give it a role in Franco-German reconciliation.
21 February–18 December 1916. At the timeline’s yearly scale, the campaign is represented by a marker within 1916.
Imperial War Museums · Somme
The Battle of the Somme

British and French forces launch an offensive against German positions on the Western Front. The hoped-for breakthrough gives way to months of costly fighting. The campaign involves successive operations, not only its devastating first day.
1 July–18 November 1916. At this scale the marker represents the year, while these dates describe the campaign.
Imperial War Museums · Korean War
The Korean War

The invasion of South Korea by North Korea expands into a war involving United Nations forces and Chinese intervention. Military advances and retreats devastate the peninsula and displace civilians. An armistice halts the main fighting while Korea remains divided.
25 June 1950–27 July 1953 covers the fighting through the armistice. An armistice is not a peace treaty.
